content: Central obesity, also referred to as apple-shaped or masculine obesity, is characterized by the predominant accumulation of body fat around the abdomen and upper body. This condition is closely associated with visceral fat, which is fat stored within the abdominal cavity and around internal organs. Central obesity is frequently observed in individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and metabolic syndrome. It is linked to a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Additionally, central obesity can be a feature of lipodystrophies, which are a group of disorders that may be inherited or caused by secondary factors, such as the use of protease inhibitors (a class of medications used in the treatment of AIDS). Central obesity is also one of the hallmark symptoms of Cushing's syndrome. Despite the colloquial terms beer belly, beer gut, or pot belly, there is limited scientific evidence to support the notion that beer consumption specifically predisposes individuals to abdominal obesity. Certain medications, such as dolutegravir and zidovudine, have been identified as potential contributors to central obesity as a side effect. The diagnosis of central obesity is typically made by measuring the waist-to-hip ratio. In women, a waist-to-hip ratio of 0.9 or higher is indicative of central obesity. The primary therapeutic approach to managing central obesity involves weight loss, particularly when the condition is considered disfiguring or when it increases the risk of associated diseases. Adjunctive pharmacological therapies may include the use of orlistat or sibutramine. In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, physicians may prefer prescribing metformin and thiazolidinediones (such as rosiglitazone or pioglitazone) as antidiabetic agents, rather than sulfonylurea derivatives. The term love handles is a colloquial expression used to describe a layer of fat deposited around the midsection, particularly visible on the sides over the external oblique muscles of the abdomen. The name love handles may derive from the idea that they provide a soft area to rest one’s hand when embracing someone or serve as a grip during moments of intimacy. Love handles are more commonly observed in men than in women, as the male body tends to store fat in the midsection. In contrast, women are more likely to accumulate fat around the hips and thighs. Love handles often become more pronounced with age, particularly as individuals approach middle age, due to decreased physical activity levels. Both men and women may feel self-conscious about the appearance of love handles, which can contribute to negative body image. While numerous products claim to target and eliminate love handles, it is widely accepted that spot reduction is not feasible. The most effective way to reduce love handles is through overall fat loss, achieved by increasing physical activity (such as engaging in cardiovascular exercise and weight training) and reducing caloric intake.
